candidates.excerpt: The idea that stringing together 5, 10, or 20 language models will spontaneously generate a super intelligence. But throwing multiple models into an unstructured workflow doesn't multiply their IQ. It just creates massive coordination noise. Every time these models talk over one another, you pay for duplicated API calls and their context windows rapidly degrade with redundant information. High performance system design focuses on the strict operational boundary the next agent actually controls rather than the raw number of models in a dashboard. To scale these systems safely, you have to separate their memory, their authority, or their action space. Unconstrained complexity is a trap. You see this trap most clearly in how developers assign human job titles to AI. They spin up a researcher, a writer, and an editor. But under the hood, all three of those roles are pulling from the exact same foundational model and sharing the identical context window. You fix this by replacing the conversational chatter with rigid role-based pipelines that exchange what software developers call typed artifacts. A typed artifact is a strictly formatted deliverable like a JSON data schema, a standard text format for data, or a code patch. candidates.excerpt: multi-agent system is not your default starting point. It is a conservative, calculated escalation of complexity. There is an anxiety running through the industry that properly engineered autonomous AI swarms are going to remove humans from the loop entirely. The reality of the architecture shows the opposite. As AI pipelines successfully automate the intermediate friction of work like data extraction and code compilation, they demand a much stronger capstone of governance. The human worker is actually formally elevated. They become a mandatory routing node positioned at the very top of the multi-agent workflow. From that position, humans apply the final policy judgments. We interpret the nuance of the outputs and grant the legal and operational approvals that algorithms simply cannot execute. Robust multi-agent design requires the deliberate decomposition of workflows, enforcing boundaries that ultimately demand a human to govern the output.
